messages.subject: Line transect straightness
parts:
Hi all, I'm a newbie and this is my first post.
I have perpendicular distance rockfish data collected on a manned
submersible survey. It is not possible to pilot the submersible in a
perfectly straight line. In fact, the transects were far from straight (we
had a DVL hooked up so we have a trackline) due to currents, etc. How
critical is it that these lines be straight? Does it help that the observers
are locked inside the sub and therefore have a limited field of view? I am
thinking not. I read Buckland et al 1993 (pp 29-36) and there are three
assumptions, one of which is not line straightness....
Cheers
Chris

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Line transect straightness
parts:
Hi Chris, list,

See Buckland et al. (2001), page 296, which refers to the work of Hiby and
Krishna (in press at the time -- now published in Biometrics 57, 727-731). I
recommend reading the paper as it is short and clearly written. Neverthess, in
summary:

There are two issues to consider.

The first is estimating the number of animals within the surveyed region. Hiby
and Krishna showed that there is no problem here, so long as (a) rather than
perpendicular distance, one measures the shortest distance between the animal
and the curving transect, and (b) the line is not too "wiggly" (there should be
few curves with radius of curvature less than the distance within which most
animals are seen). In your case, perhaps the line is almost straight, in which
case you will probably find that (a) perpendicular distance and shortest
distance are almost identical so using the former is no problem, and (b) is
satisfied without any problems.

The second issue is extrapolating from the number in the surveyed region to the
number in the study area. Many curved transects are curved in terrestrial
surveys because they are on existing trails. Then the region surveyed is not a
random sample of the study area and there is no statistical basis to extrapolate
the density in the surveyed region to that in the whole area. In your case, if
your lines were laid out according to a randomized design (e.g., systematic
random), and departures from the designed line locations are likely to be
uncorrelated with animal density (i.e., you don't tend to get "pushed" into
regions of high density by undersea currents) then you can ignore this issue.
If you did survey the region nonrandomly, then you're going to have to go to
great lengths to get an unbiased estimate of density (see Buckland et al. or
Hiby and Krishna for more on this).

Hope this helps,

- Len

messages.author: a4f1c1f368222651
messages.subject: Re: Line transect straightness
parts:
Thanks Len, everybody:
Krishna sent me the paper you refer to and I think this analysis should be
straightforward. My transect lines are the same transect lines followed 20
years ago by other researchers, who designed a randomized survey. The only
problem perhaps is that the sub moves very slowly and the port & starboard
thrusters tend to spin the whole sub about the Z-axis, while stopped. This
makes the path very "wiggly" on paper but since I was personally inside the
sub, I can say that it does not affect the counts. These fish move very,
very slowly and are not disturbed by the sub. They move so little in fact
that we can say with near certainty that we did not count a fish more than
once.

I have one more question - is it common to want to seperate the data by
substrate type prior to running distance on the data? e.g. I have a database
containing observations for a certain species of rockfish, and the substrate
type it was observed over (bedrock, cobble, gravel, etc.). I run a query to
extract the observations over bedrock and then run distance on that data. So
I get density measurements for different substrate types. The output seems
reasonable, i.e. density over muddy bottom is way less than density over
cobble, as it should be for rockfish....

Thanks for the reply,
Cheers
Chris

On Mon, 17 May 2004 16:12:46 +0100, Chris Grandin wrote:

> >I have one more question - is it common to want to seperate the data by
> >substrate type prior to running distance on the data? e.g. I have a database
> >containing observations for a certain species of rockfish, and the substrate
> >type it was observed over (bedrock, cobble, gravel, etc.). I run a query to
> >extract the observations over bedrock and then run distance on that data. So
> >I get density measurements for different substrate types. The output seems
> >reasonable, i.e. density over muddy bottom is way less than density over
> >cobble, as it should be for rockfish....

Hi Chris, list,

Yes, it is common to want to do this, and no problem in getting the substrate-
specific estimates. You may want to get all the data at once and make substrate a
stratum, so you can investigate whether to fit a pooled detection function or a
separate one for each substrate (or substrate as a covariate in the MCDS engine).
You can ask for density estimates by stratum (ie by substrate). Remember though,
if you want to compare them (for example to see if there are "statistically
significant" differences -- or to compare confidence limits) that they are not
statistically independent because they often share the same transect line -- for
more on this, see the message I posted earlier today to Sally Archibald.

Cheers,

- Len
